office.title: Indiana School Board Member
office.summary: A school board is the elected or appointed governing body of a public school corporation, the legal unit that runs a local school district [1, 2]. The board hires and evaluates the superintendent, adopts policies, and approves the annual budget, while the superintendent and staff run schools day to day [3]. Most boards have five or seven members serving staggered four-year terms [3]. Starting in 2026, candidates may list a political party, run as independents, or list no affiliation on the ballot, and there is no primary for these seats [2, 4].

facts.label: Term
facts.value: 4 years, with elections staggered so part of the board is chosen every two years [3]

facts.label: Elected
facts.value: At the November general election (November 3, 2026, or November 2028 for some seats); depending on the local organization plan, members represent the whole school corporation (at large) or a district within it, and some boards are wholly or partly appointed [2]

facts.label: Ballot label
facts.value: Each candidate chooses a party label, 'Independent', or no affiliation, shown next to the name; no primary and no straight-ticket voting for these races [2, 4]

facts.label: Pay
facts.value: Set by board resolution: an annual amount of no more than 10% of the lowest starting teacher salary in the school corporation, plus a capped per diem [5]

duties: Hires, evaluates and can dismiss the superintendent, and approves the hiring and firing of principals, teachers and other staff recommended by the superintendent [1, 7, 3].
Adopts the annual budget, appropriates funds and oversees school finances [1, 3].

Decides whether to ask voters to approve an operating referendum (an extra property tax levy); the board adopts the resolution and the Department of Local Government Finance reviews the ballot language for compliance with state law [8].
Approves contracts, buys and sells property, and decides on construction, repair and demolition of school buildings [1].

Bargains with the teachers' union over salary, wages and wage-related benefits such as health insurance and retirement; state law excludes teacher evaluation procedures from those bargaining subjects [9].
Writes and updates policies and rules for schools, often in a policy handbook, including the student handbook [1, 3].
Buys curricular materials, provides them to students without charge, and runs programs such as student transportation and school lunch [1].

Must adopt a process for parents and residents to ask that library material be removed as obscene or harmful to minors, review requests at public meetings and keep a public catalog of library materials [10].
Hears written appeals of student expulsions, unless the board has voted not to hear them [11].
Must take official action openly; Indiana's Open Door Law says public agencies' official action is to be conducted openly so the people may be fully informed [12, 13].

A school board member must have lived in the school corporation (and, for a district seat, the district) for at least one year before the election, and a teacher or other employee of the school corporation may not serve on its board [2].

What the board does not control: the State Board of Education adopts statewide academic standards [14], the General Assembly sets the state school funding formula in the state budget [15], and voucher (Choice Scholarship) eligibility is set by state law [16].
recent_changes: 2025: Senate Enrolled Act 287 allowed school board candidates to declare a party affiliation; the Indiana School Boards Association opposed the change, and a supporter quoted by WNDU, a Noblesville school board member, said it adds transparency [17].

2026: Candidates choose a party, 'Independent' or no affiliation on their nominating petition, and that choice appears on the ballot; a candidate claiming the Democratic or Republican party must have voted in that party's primary in the two most recent primaries they voted in, or have certification from the county party chair, or can be challenged and removed from the ballot [2].

July 2026: Chalkbeat reported, citing Indiana School Boards Association data, that 524 of 1,044 candidates chose a party, about 72% of them Republicans [18]; the Indiana Election Division's 2026 guidance and the wording of the law differ on the primary-voting test, a question county election boards decide [19].

February 2026: Senate Enrolled Act 25 set the order of school board candidates on the ballot, grouped by party, with candidates who list no affiliation placed after the party and independent candidates [20].

2025: Senate Enrolled Act 1, a property tax law, limits how much operating revenue districts can raise through taxes and restricts school referendums to statewide general elections in even-numbered years [21, 22].
2025: The same law requires districts to share operating revenue with brick-and-mortar charter schools that enroll their students, statewide starting in 2028 [21, 22].
2025: The state budget opened Choice Scholarship vouchers to all Indiana families starting in June 2026 [16].
2026: The Indianapolis Public Education Corporation, rather than the Indianapolis Public Schools board, now certifies Indianapolis Public Schools referendum questions for the ballot [20].

2023: Senate Enrolled Act 391 changed the so-called $1 law so the Indiana Department of Education can order districts that lost at least 10% of enrollment over five years to close schools under 60% capacity and offer them to charter schools [23].
2023: House Enrolled Act 1447 required school districts to set up procedures for complaints that library material is obscene or harmful to minors [10].

race_context: Zionsville Community Schools (ZCS) serves Zionsville and Eagle and Union townships in Boone County, with a high school, two middle schools and six elementary schools [24]. The district counted 7,852 students on the Oct. 1, 2025 count day, up 28 from the prior year [25]. Rebecca Coffman is superintendent [26].

The Board of School Trustees has five elected members representing Eagle and Union townships [24], serving four-year terms [27]. Current members: Katie Aeschliman (president), Michael Berg (vice president), Michael Coussens (secretary), Jennifer Valentine and Christy Wessel-Powell [24]. In 2022 the IndyStar reported that any registered voter in the district may vote in each seat's race regardless of where they live [28].

Three seats are on the Nov. 3, 2026 ballot, one per race (at-large, Eagle Township and Union Township), matching the state list's "vote for 1" [27, 6]. All three incumbents are running: Wessel-Powell (at-large), Berg (Eagle) and Valentine (Union), each first elected or reelected in 2022 [27, 28]. Each faces one challenger; the three challengers are listed as Republicans and the incumbents with no party [6, 27]. The other two seats (Aeschliman, Eagle; Coussens, Union) were elected in 2024 and are not on the ballot [27].

Referendum: on June 8, 2026, the board voted 4-0 (Coussens absent) to place an eight-year operating referendum on the November ballot, renewing a levy first approved in 2012 and last renewed in 2019 that expires in December 2027 [29, 26]. The question sets a maximum rate of 0.4128 per $100 of assessed value and a maximum annual levy of $21,463,325; state-required ballot language says a $600,000 median home's tax bill would rise $1,368 a year, which the state approved on June 10 [30].

The superintendent says the referendum pays for about one in three ZCS teachers, that 100% of its revenue goes to teacher salaries and benefits, and that ZCS is the lowest-funded Indiana district per pupil; she says the required ballot figure is calculated as if no referendum existed and will appear higher than what residents would actually pay [26]. The parent group YES for ZCS calls it a renewal, not a new tax, and estimates an average change of $7.10 a year for a median residence [31].

Budget and SEA 1: the district says the 2025 property-tax law (SEA 1) reduces the taxable value of homes, so school revenue from them is expected to fall even as home values rise, and that because the current levy expires in December 2027 and referendums may now appear only in even-year November elections, waiting until 2028 would be too late [26].

Facilities and growth: in spring 2026 ZCS broke ground on an Early Learning Center that will also house administrative offices; the district says this lets it accommodate growth without opening a new elementary or middle school for now and frees space at the high school [32]. Class-size targets are 18 in kindergarten and first grade, 20 in grades 2-3 and 25 in grades 4-12 [25].
Accountability: in August 2025 district staff briefed the board on the state's proposed new accountability and grading model taking effect in fall 2026 [33].

Forums: no joint school board candidate forum was found in reviewed sources; the Zionsville Village Residents Association scheduled a presentation by Superintendent Coffman on the referendum for Oct. 11, 2026 [34]. Of the six candidates, Valentine and Waters said they support the referendum, and all three incumbents voted to place it on the ballot [35, 36, 29].

candidates.summary: Incumbent at-large member, first elected in 2022; a Purdue education professor and ZCS parent, she is listed with no party [27, 6, 37].
background: Was an assistant professor of literacy and language education at Purdue University as of 2022; holds a Ph.D. in education from Indiana University Bloomington and was earlier a K-2 classroom teacher and literacy coach, according to her 2022 campaign site [37].
Parent of two children in ZCS, per her 2022 campaign site [37].
path_to_ballot: Listed with no party on the 2026 ballot [6].
Won the at-large seat in 2022 over Matthew Keefer and Sarah Sampson; sworn in January 2023 [27, 28].

items: Voted with the 4-0 majority on June 8, 2026, to place the operating referendum on the ballot [29].
In 2022 she campaigned on giving teachers support and autonomy, maintaining student safety and managing district growth [28].

on_incumbent: Is a current board member [24]. No 2026 statement on the board's record was found in reviewed sources.
plans: Her 2022 campaign site pledged to support teachers, welcome all families and provide responsible stewardship of the schools [37].
endorsements_finance: In 2022 she was endorsed by then-board president Debbie Ungar [28]. No 2026 endorsements or campaign finance reports were found in reviewed sources.
gaps: No 2026 campaign platform, interview or Ballotpedia survey was found; her listed campaign website dates from 2022.
Unverified (search snippet only): a June 22, 2026 Current in Zionsville article reported the three incumbents seeking reelection; the article could not be fetched (site blocked).
Current job title (assistant vs. associate professor) not verified for 2026.
Campaign finance filings with Boone County were not reviewed.

candidates.summary: Engineer, small-business owner and ZCS parent running for the at-large seat, listed as a Republican [38, 39, 6].
background: Has a bachelor's degree in engineering from Penn State and a master's in engineering from Purdue; worked in product development for a local Fortune 500 company [39].
Zionsville resident since 2015; he and his wife own several Zionsville-based businesses; parent of three ZCS students [39].
Says he has coached Zionsville Little League, served on his HOA board and volunteered with the Zionsville Food Pantry, Wheeler Mission and Safe Families [39, 38].
path_to_ballot: Listed as a Republican on the 2026 ballot list [6]. First run for this office found in reviewed sources [38].

items: Says ZCS's budget "has grown exponentially over the last decade while student growth and academic success have moderated," and wants to fully understand district finances and direct dollars to students' learning needs [38].
Lists financial audits among procedures the district should adopt [38].
Says a sound budget prioritizes competitive teacher pay and classroom support, and that he would reduce "unnecessary administrative burdens" on teachers [38, 40].
Wants the board to set high academic goals and "stretch targets" for administrators, prioritizing math, reading and science [38, 40].
His website lists "Classrooms and curriculum should remain neutral" and "Parents are the decision makers in their children's education" among top issues [40].
Calls for structured, accessible ways for parents, teachers and taxpayers to be heard, and for the board to consult outside experts as well as those recommended by administrators [38].

on_incumbent: Says the board needs members who collaborate with experts beyond those recommended by the administration [38]. No direct comment on specific board votes was found.
plans: Says he would seek and debate options on financial and curricular decisions and focus on safety, financial audits, student support and educational resources [40, 38].
endorsements_finance: Said in his Aug. 26, 2026 Ballotpedia survey that he had not accepted any endorsement [38]. No campaign finance reports were found in reviewed sources.
gaps: No stated position on the 2026 operating referendum was found.
Unverified (search snippet only): Current in Zionsville reported in July 2026 that he did not respond to interview requests.
Campaign finance filings with Boone County were not reviewed.

candidates.summary: Former elementary teacher and ZCS parent challenging the Eagle Township incumbent, listed as a Republican [41, 6].
background: Has a B.A. in education from Purdue; taught for nine years (second and third grades at a charter school, then fourth and fifth grades at a public school) and has substituted in ZCS and nearby districts [41].
Moved to Zionsville in 2017; parent of two ZCS students; has volunteered with Boone County CASA and school PTOs [41].
path_to_ballot: Listed as a Republican on the 2026 ballot list [6].

items: Says she plans to support the referendum to protect class sizes, but that if it passes the district should pursue independent financial audits and keep administrative costs as low as possible [36].
Supports more recess for middle schoolers, more textbooks and paper-based learning "where appropriate," hands-on learning and academic competition [36].
Wants a rigorous writing curriculum, explicit grammar instruction and mastery of foundational math in elementary grades [36].
Lists retaining and attracting excellent educators as a focus [36].

Says classrooms should remain politically neutral, and that students' broader social, emotional and medical needs should be addressed by parents and outside professionals rather than school resources [36].

on_incumbent: Her calls for independent audits and lower administrative costs imply changes to current practice, but no direct comment on the board's record was found [36].
plans: Says she would focus on student achievement, partnering with families and educators, and stewardship of taxpayer money [41].
endorsements_finance: No endorsements or campaign finance reports were found in reviewed sources.
gaps: Unverified (search snippet only): Current in Zionsville reported in July 2026 that this is her first run for public office and that she favors less emphasis on laptops and Chromebooks.
Campaign finance filings with Boone County were not reviewed.

candidates.summary: Incumbent Eagle Township member and board vice president seeking a third term; listed with no party [24, 6, 28].
background: As of 2022, a licensed therapist and program manager for HIV services at a large health network [28].
Parent of two daughters in ZCS as of 2022 [28].
path_to_ballot: Listed with no party on the 2026 ballot [6].
Joined the board in 2018 and won the Eagle Township seat in 2022 over Timothy Hardt [28, 27].

items: Voted with the 4-0 majority on June 8, 2026, to place the operating referendum on the ballot [29].
In 2022 he campaigned on responsible management of tax dollars and teacher autonomy in the classroom [28].

on_incumbent: Is a current board member and its vice president [24]. No 2026 statement on the board's record was found in fetched sources.
plans: No 2026 platform was found in fetched sources.
endorsements_finance: Endorsed by the Zionsville Educators Association, per Ballotpedia [42]. No campaign finance reports were found in reviewed sources.
gaps: His campaign Facebook page (Berg4Board) could not be read.
Unverified (search snippet only): Current in Zionsville reported in July 2026 that he backs the district's referendum.
Campaign finance filings with Boone County were not reviewed.

candidates.summary: Incumbent Union Township member first elected in 2022, listed with no party; endorsed by the Zionsville Educators Association [35, 6].
background: Has a bachelor's degree from Oakland University [35].
Parent of two ZCS graduates and two current students; her family is in its 13th school year in Zionsville [35].
Says she volunteers with sports, robotics, the civics bee and other community programs [35].
path_to_ballot: Listed with no party on the 2026 ballot [6].
Won the Union Township seat in 2022 in a three-way race with Michael Coussens and Marcus Such [27, 28].

items: Supports the operating referendum and says she is running to continue the board's fiscal stewardship [35].
Voted with the 4-0 majority on June 8, 2026, to place the referendum on the ballot [29].
Calls for strategic investment in teachers and staff, and says retention is vital [35].
Lists responsible planning for growth, including land and capital needs [35].
Lists student safety, mental health and inclusion as top priorities [35].
Wants clear channels for parent feedback and decision-making in which the community can see the steps taken [35].

on_incumbent: Is a current board member [24]. Describes the board as "collaborative, with diverse strengths" and says Zionsville is ranked No. 2 among Indiana public school districts and should aim for No. 1 [35].
plans: Says she will focus on K-12 academic standards, early childhood development and vocational training, and on prioritizing spending that directly affects student outcomes [35].
endorsements_finance: Endorsed by the Zionsville Educators Association, per her Ballotpedia survey [35]. No campaign finance reports were found in reviewed sources.
gaps: The ranking she cites (No. 2 in Indiana) was not independently verified; its source was not stated.
Current occupation not stated in 2026 sources.
Campaign finance filings with Boone County were not reviewed.

candidates.summary: Nonprofit event planner and ZCS parent challenging the Union Township incumbent, listed as a Republican [43, 6].
background: Has a bachelor's degree in communications from Grace College and works as an event planner for a local nonprofit [43].
Built a home in Zionsville in 2016; parent of three children in ZCS elementary, middle and high schools; has coached Zionsville Little League sports [43].
path_to_ballot: Listed as a Republican on the 2026 ballot list [6].

items: Says the largest possible share of school funding should go to teachers and classroom learning, with streamlined administrative costs [44].
Wants administrators to give teachers more help with classroom behavior to protect instructional time, and supports strategic use of teacher aides, especially in larger classes [44].
Says classrooms should stay politically impartial and that students' social, emotional and medical needs should be led by families and outside professionals [44].

Says the health and sex-education curriculum should cover nutrition, physical development and fitness, and that instruction on condom use, sexually transmitted diseases and the causes of pregnancy is not appropriate in public school; supports requiring explicit parental approval for health curriculum materials [44].

on_incumbent: Her proposals on health curriculum and behavior support imply changes to current practice, but no direct comment on the board's record was found [44].
plans: Lists prioritizing academic instruction, classroom-focused funding and protected instructional time [44].
endorsements_finance: No endorsements or campaign finance reports were found in reviewed sources.
gaps: No stated position on the 2026 operating referendum was found.
Unverified (search snippet only): Current in Zionsville reported in July 2026 that she declined an interview.
Campaign finance filings with Boone County were not reviewed.
